title: Whose cutoff wins?
hook: The model never sees anyone's group. So it treats everyone the same. Right?

knows: that a model learns from examples
pass/fail cutoffs on a test score
doesNotKnow: that training minimises the average mistake over whoever is in the data
that an under-represented group can carry most of the errors

misconception: If you do not give a model the group label, it treats everyone equally.
objective: The learner can explain that a model trained to make the fewest total mistakes fits the majority of its data, so a group that is rare in training can bear the errors even though the model never sees group labels.

claims.text: The toy has 100 invented people: 90 in group A, qualified from a score of 50, and 10 in group B, qualified from 30. Scores are spread evenly from 0 to 100 (9 group A people and 1 group B person in each band of 10 points).
claims.source: The lesson's own data in Demo.tsx (A_SCORES, B_SCORES, A_LINE, B_LINE).

claims.text: A mistake is passing someone who is not qualified or failing someone who is. One cutoff applies to everyone; the model learns the cutoff (in steps of 10) with the fewest total mistakes.
The fewest total mistakes come at a cutoff of 50, group A's line: 2 mistakes in 100 (98% right), both group B people scoring 30–50 who are wrongly failed. That is 20% of group B and 0% of group A.
claims.source: Running mistakes() from Demo.tsx for cutoffs 0–100: totals 48, 38, 28, 18, 10, 2, 12, 22, 32, 42, 52; minimum at 50 with A 0, B 2. Continuous version: expected mistakes ∝ 0.9·|c − 50| + 0.1·|c − 30|, whose slope between 30 and 50 is −0.9 + 0.1 < 0, so it falls until c = 50.

claims.text: At a cutoff of 40 there are 10 mistakes, 9 in group A and 1 in group B. Going from 40 to 50 breaks one group B person and fixes nine group A people, so the total drops and training lands on 50.
claims.source: The 40–50 band holds 9 group A people (not qualified, below 50) who a cutoff of 40 wrongly passes, and 1 group B person (score 45, qualified) whom it now correctly passes. mistakes(40) in Demo.tsx = A 9, B 1 (the remaining B mistake is the person at 35, still failed). | REVISION v2 2026-10-14: text edited to match stage; needs re-check. | v3 2026-10-14 (demo-builder): reveal now quotes mistakes(40) computed live (A 9, B 1, total 10) and runs the comparison 40 -> 50 instead of 50 -> 40. The gate's 'at-40' milestone now needs the cutoff to rest at 40 for 300 ms, so the reveal's 'You stopped at 40' is true. Reopened. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 21): Own copy of mistakes(): 40 -> A 9, B 1 (B at 35), total 10; 50 -> A 0, B 2 (35, 45). 40 -> 50 breaks B at 45, fixes nine A in 40-50. The reveal's 'You stopped at 40' is guaranteed by the 300 ms 'at-40' milestone.

claims.text: About real systems: commercial face-analysis tools misclassified the gender of darker-skinned women far more often than that of lighter-skinned men (error rates up to 34.7% versus at most 0.8%).
claims.source: Buolamwini & Gebru 2018, “Gender Shades: Intersectional Accuracy Disparities in Commercial Gender Classification”, Proceedings of Machine Learning Research 81 (FAT* 2018), abstract (34.7% and 0.8% maximum error rates).

claims.text: Each press of 'Let the model learn a step' moves the cutoff 10 points toward the lowest total, and the stage reports the total before and after (30→40: 18→10; 40→50: 10→2).
claims.source: step() and message() in Demo.tsx; totals from mistakes() (see c3: 18 at 30, 10 at 40, 2 at 50). Stand-in for the doesNotKnow item 'training minimises the average mistake'. Added v3 2026-10-14 by demo-builder. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 21): step(): +10 if cut < BEST else -10, disabled at BEST (50). Totals 0..100: 48, 38, 28, 18, 10, 2, 12, 22, 32, 42, 52 (falls monotonically toward 50 from both sides), so 30->40: 18->10 and 40->50: 10->2 as message() prints.

recall.question: A hiring model is trained on past applicants, 95% from one city. Nobody's city is in the data it sees. Where are its mistakes likely to fall?
options: Mostly on applicants from other places
Evenly on everyone, since it never sees the city
recall.why: Training minimises total mistakes, and the majority dominates the total. If the rare group differs, the rule fits the majority and the rare group carries the errors.
